steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a machine learning paper arguing that language modeling is compression: explain the link between prediction and lossless compression, why large pre-trained Transformers suit offline compression, and summarize the work and its contributions in subsections.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Information theory, machine learning and the model-compression equivalence
- Arithmetic coding and Transformers as compressors (online vs. offline)
- Context length as a limiting factor
## This Work
- Compression as a lens on foundation models; summary of findings
## Contributions
- List of contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Equivalence
  - information theory and machine learning "two sides of the same coin"
  - probabilistic models of data <-> lossless compression
  - source coding theorem: expected message length in bits of optimal entropy encoder = negative \log_{2} -likelihood
  - maximizing \log_{2} -likelihood = minimizing bits per message
  - ways: Huffman coding, arithmetic coding, asymmetric numeral systems
- Arithmetic coding + Transformers
  - arithmetic coding optimal in coding length -> performance depends on probabilistic model (Fig. 1)
  - large pre-trained Transformers, foundation models, successful on many predictive tasks
  - Transformer-based compression with arithmetic coding: state of the art online and offline
  - online: pseudo-randomly initialized model trained on the stream itself
  - offline (ours): trained on external dataset, then compresses (potentially different) stream; in-context, fixed parameters
  - in-context learning abilities -> suited for offline compression
- Context length
  - limits max bytes compressed at a time
  - only a few kilobytes (each "token" 2 or 3 bytes), lots of compute
  - long-context tasks (algorithmic reasoning, long-term memory); extending context lengths gaining attention
  - in-context compression view -> insight into failure modes
## This Work
- advocate lossless compression to study foundation models
- empirical study of offline (in-context) compression of large language models; readily available, no training overhead
- trained mostly on text, competitive rates across modalities; beat domain-specific compressors (ignoring parameter size)
- scaling laws hold for compression; adjusted compression rate adds twist: scaling beyond a point hurts since parameters count
- prediction through compression lens encompasses generalization: compresses well -> generalizes well
## Contributions
- review compression via arithmetic coding; link language modeling and compression
- LLMs compress other modalities well: Chinchilla 70B 43.4% on ImageNet patches, 16.4% on LibriSpeech; beats PNG (58.5%), FLAC (30.3%)
- scaling laws: dataset size limits model size; scaling not a silver bullet
- compressors as generative models; visual illustration
- tokenization = pre-compression; doesn't improve compression in general, but more information in context -> better prediction

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Information theory and machine learning are linked very closely and people have even called them “two sides of the same coin”. One elegant connection is that probabilistic models of data and lossless compression are essentially equivalent. The fundamental theorem that describes this idea is the source coding theorem, which says that the expected message length in bits of an optimal entropy encoder is equal to the negative \log_{2} -likelihood of the statistical model. So maximizing the \log_{2} -likelihood (of the data) is the same as minimizing the number of bits needed per message. Lossless compression with a probabilistic model can be done in a lot of different ways, for example Huffman coding, arithmetic coding and asymmetric numeral systems.

Arithmetic coding is known to be optimal in coding length, which means that how well the compression works overall depends on how capable the probabilistic model is (Fig. 1 gives an overview of arithmetic coding). In recent years, large pre-trained Transformers, the so-called foundation models, have been very successful on a wide range of predictive tasks, so they are promising candidates to use with arithmetic coding. Transformer-based compression with arithmetic coding has in fact produced state-of-the-art results in the online and in the offline settings. In the online setting a model that is pseudo-randomly initialized is trained directly on the stream of data to be compressed. The offline setting, which is the one we consider in our work, trains the model on an external dataset first and then uses it to compress a (potentially different) data stream. So offline compression is done in-context, with a fixed set of model parameters. Transformers have shown impressive in-context learning abilities, so they are ideally suited for offline compression.

The context length is a key limiting factor in offline compression, because it decides the maximum number of bytes a model can compress at one time. Transformers can only compress a few kilobytes (each “token” is coded with 2 or 3 bytes), and they need a lot of compute. Many challenging predictive tasks (for example algorithmic reasoning or long-term memory) need long contexts, so extending the context lengths of these models is a key challenge that is getting more attention. Looking at it as in-context compression gives insights into the failure modes of current foundation models.

## This Work
- advocate (lossless) compression to study foundation models
- empirical study of offline (in-context) compression of large language models; readily available, no training overhead
- mostly text-trained, but competitive across modalities; beat domain-specific compressors (ignoring parameter size)
- scaling laws hold for compression, but adjusted rates: scaling beyond a point hurts
- compression encompasses generalization
## Contributions
- review arithmetic coding with predictive models; language modeling <-> compression
- Chinchilla 70B: 43.4% ImageNet patches, 16.4% LibriSpeech; beats PNG (58.5%), FLAC (30.3%)
- dataset size limits model size; scaling not a silver bullet
- compressors as generative models
- tokenization as pre-compression: no compression gain, better prediction

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Information theory and machine learning are linked very closely and people have even called them “two sides of the same coin”. One elegant connection is that probabilistic models of data and lossless compression are essentially equivalent. The fundamental theorem that describes this idea is the source coding theorem, which says that the expected message length in bits of an optimal entropy encoder is equal to the negative \log_{2} -likelihood of the statistical model. So maximizing the \log_{2} -likelihood (of the data) is the same as minimizing the number of bits needed per message. Lossless compression with a probabilistic model can be done in a lot of different ways, for example Huffman coding, arithmetic coding and asymmetric numeral systems.

Arithmetic coding is known to be optimal in coding length, which means that how well the compression works overall depends on how capable the probabilistic model is (Fig. 1 gives an overview of arithmetic coding). In recent years, large pre-trained Transformers, the so-called foundation models, have been very successful on a wide range of predictive tasks, so they are promising candidates to use with arithmetic coding. Transformer-based compression with arithmetic coding has in fact produced state-of-the-art results in the online and in the offline settings. In the online setting a model that is pseudo-randomly initialized is trained directly on the stream of data to be compressed. The offline setting, which is the one we consider in our work, trains the model on an external dataset first and then uses it to compress a (potentially different) data stream. So offline compression is done in-context, with a fixed set of model parameters. Transformers have shown impressive in-context learning abilities, so they are ideally suited for offline compression.

The context length is a key limiting factor in offline compression, because it decides the maximum number of bytes a model can compress at one time. Transformers can only compress a few kilobytes (each “token” is coded with 2 or 3 bytes), and they need a lot of compute. Many challenging predictive tasks (for example algorithmic reasoning or long-term memory) need long contexts, so extending the context lengths of these models is a key challenge that is getting more attention. Looking at it as in-context compression gives insights into the failure modes of current foundation models.

## This Work

We argue for using (lossless) compression to study foundation models. For that we do an extensive empirical investigation of the offline (in-context) compression capabilities of large language models, since they are now readily available and so they can be used for compression without the training overhead. We show empirically that these models, even though they were (meta-)trained mainly on text, get competitive compression rates across different data modalities, and they outperform domain-specific standard compressors (if model parameter size is not counted). We also shed new light on scaling laws and show that they also hold for compression, but measuring the adjusted compression rates instead of the log loss adds a twist: scaling beyond a certain point makes compression performance worse because the model parameters have to be accounted for in the compressed output. Finally, we argue for framing (self-supervised) prediction through the lens of compression because it encompasses generalization: a model that compresses well generalizes well.

## Contributions

We study the lossless compression capabilities of foundation models empirically:

- • We review how predictive models can compress via arithmetic coding and point out the connection between current language modeling research and compression.

- • We show that large language models get impressive compression rates (not counting model parameter size) on modalities other than text. For example, Chinchilla 70B gets compression rates of 43.4% on ImageNet patches and 16.4% on LibriSpeech samples, and it beats domain-specific compressors like PNG (58.5%) or FLAC (30.3%), respectively.

- • We revisit scaling laws and show that the dataset size is a hard limit on model size in terms of compression performance, and that scaling the model is not a silver bullet.

- • We use the compression-prediction equivalence to employ compressors as generative models and to visually illustrate how the underlying compressor performs.

- • We show that tokenization, which can be seen as a pre-compression, does not in general improve compression performance, but it lets models increase the information content in their context, so it is generally used to improve prediction performance.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Information theory and machine learning are inextricably linked and have even been called “two sides of the same coin” [1]. A particularly elegant connection is the essential equivalence between probabilistic models of data and lossless compression. The source coding theorem [2] is the fundamental theorem describing this idea: the expected message length in bits of an optimal entropy encoder equals the negative \log_{2} -likelihood of the statistical model. In other words, maximizing the \log_{2} -likelihood (of the data) is equivalent to minimizing the number of bits required per message. Lossless compression with a probabilistic model can be achieved in a variety of ways, including Huffman coding [3], arithmetic coding [4,5], and asymmetric numeral systems [6].

Arithmetic coding in particular is known to be optimal in terms of coding length, so the overall compression performance depends on the capabilities of the probabilistic model (see Fig. 1 for an overview of arithmetic coding). In recent years, large pre-trained Transformers [7], so-called foundation models [8], have proven highly successful across a wide range of predictive tasks [9,10] and are thus promising candidates for use with arithmetic coding. Indeed, Transformer-based compression with arithmetic coding has produced state-of-the-art results in both the online [11,12] and offline settings [13]. In the online setting, a pseudo-randomly initialized model is trained directly on the stream of data to be compressed, whereas the offline setting, which we consider in our work, trains the model on an external dataset before using it to compress a (potentially different) data stream. Offline compression is therefore performed in-context, with a fixed set of model parameters. Transformers have demonstrated impressive in-context learning abilities [14,15,16,17] and are thus ideally suited for offline compression.

The context length is a key limiting factor in offline compression, as it dictates the maximum number of bytes a model can compress at a time. Transformers can only compress a few kilobytes (each “token” being coded with 2 or 3 bytes) while requiring a lot of compute. Many challenging predictive tasks (e.g., algorithmic reasoning or long-term memory) require long contexts [18], and extending these models’ context lengths is thus a key challenge that is gaining increased attention [19,20,21]. The in-context compression view offers insights into the failure modes of current foundation models.

## This Work

We advocate using (lossless) compression to study foundation models. To that end, we conduct an extensive empirical investigation of the offline (in-context) compression capabilities of large language models, reasoning that they have become readily available [22,23] and can thus be used for compression without training overhead. We demonstrate empirically that these models, although (meta-)trained primarily on text, achieve competitive compression rates across data modalities, outperforming domain-specific standard compressors (not accounting for model parameter size). Moreover, we shed new light on scaling laws [24], showing that they also hold for compression, but that measuring adjusted compression rates instead of log loss adds a twist: scaling beyond a certain point deteriorates compression performance, since the model parameters need to be accounted for in the compressed output. Finally, we advocate framing (self-supervised) prediction through the lens of compression, as it encompasses generalization: a model that compresses well generalizes well [25].

## Contributions

We empirically study the lossless compression capabilities of foundation models:

- • We review how to compress with predictive models via arithmetic coding and draw attention to the connection between current language modeling research and compression.

- • We show that large language models achieve impressive compression rates (disregarding model parameter size) on modalities other than text. For example, Chinchilla 70B achieves compression rates of 43.4% on ImageNet patches and 16.4% on LibriSpeech samples, beating domain-specific compressors such as PNG (58.5%) or FLAC (30.3%), respectively.

- • We revisit scaling laws, showing that dataset size places a hard limit on model size in terms of compression performance and that model scaling is not a silver bullet.

- • We leverage the compression-prediction equivalence to use compressors as generative models and to visually illustrate the performance of the underlying compressor.

- • We demonstrate that tokenization, which can be viewed as pre-compression, does not in general improve compression performance, but lets models increase the information content in their context and is therefore generally employed to improve prediction performance.
